around.headline: IISc BTech student dies by suicide in hostel room, note points to academic stress
around.summary: A BTech student at IISc was found dead in his hostel room; police say a handwritten note points to academic pressure. If you or someone you know is struggling, Tele-MANAS (dial 14416) is a free, confidential 24/7 mental health helpline.
around.source: Deccan Herald, The Hindu, The Times of India

around.summary: Three people died in unrelated road accidents around the city. A reminder to slow down and use protective gear, especially on wet roads with today's rain.

around.headline: Green Line metro frequency cut tonight for trial runs
around.summary: BMRCL is thinning out Green Line frequency tonight as it runs new trainsets ahead of CMRS inspection trials on August 12–14. If you're travelling on the Green Line late tonight, budget extra waiting time.
around.source: The Hindu, Moneycontrol, Public TV English

around.headline: Minor fire breaks out at Nagasandra Metro Station
around.summary: A small fire was reported at Nagasandra Metro Station; extent of disruption isn't yet clear. If your route passes through this station, check for delays before heading out.

around.headline: Nearly half of Bengaluru's voters flagged for deletion — verify by August 8
around.summary: Close to half of Bengaluru's 1.03 crore registered voters are flagged for possible removal in the draft SIR electoral roll. You have until tomorrow, August 8, to verify your details and avoid being struck off.
around.source: NDTV, The Times of India, Deccan Herald

around.summary: Parliament passed a bill authorising the government to permit banks to charge fees on UPI transactions, which have been free for most users so far. Watch your bank's notifications in the coming months — a free habit may start costing you per transaction.

street_smart.title: Your landlord shows up unannounced, annoyed that rent is 3 days late, and says he'll have the caretaker cut your water supply by tomorrow morning if you don't pay. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Evergreen rotation topic (tenant/landlord rights) — today's real Bengaluru safety stories (a student's death by suicide, fatal road accidents) don't fit the trap-scenario format responsibly, and no other incident in today's feeds gave enough mechanism detail. Recent evergreen and news topics already covered UPI fraud, medical emergency response, loan-app harassment, credit-card skimming, consumer court basics, two-wheeler theft, auto/cab overcharging, and digital-arrest scams within the last 3 weeks; tenant/landlord rights hasn't appeared in that window.
street_smart.situation: Rent is due but you paid it 3 days late after being away. Your landlord turns up at your door, irritated, and says that if you don't pay by tomorrow morning he'll get the building caretaker to shut off your water supply until you do. There's no written notice — just a verbal threat. What do you do?

choices.text: Pack up and move out that same night to avoid a scene, without getting your deposit settled in writing.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Leaving under threat with no written settlement hands the landlord an easy excuse to withhold your deposit later — 'you left in a hurry, so we deducted for X' — and you're left with no paper trail to dispute it.

choices.text: Threaten to call the police on him right away, without first trying to resolve it directly.
choices.feedback: Risky. Jumping straight to threats can turn a fixable rent-timing issue into a hostile standoff. A calmer, documented approach usually resolves faster and keeps both the relationship and your deposit intact.

choices.text: Ignore the warning completely, assuming no landlord would actually cut off water over a few days' delay.
choices.feedback: Risky. Some landlords do go ahead with illegal shutoffs to pressure tenants — treating the threat as empty can leave you without water with no plan in place.

choices.text: Pay what you owe (or commit to a clear date in writing) via a traceable method, get an acknowledgment, and calmly note that deliberately cutting water or power to force out a tenant is illegal harassment, not a landlord's right.
choices.feedback: Correct. Paying — or committing in writing — resolves the actual dispute, and knowing that forced utility cutoffs are illegal gives you real leverage. Most landlords back off once they know you know your rights and there's a record of the conversation.

takeaways: Never let a rent dispute rest on a verbal exchange — pay via UPI or bank transfer, not cash, so there's always a record, and ask for a receipt or written acknowledgment either way.
Willfully cutting water, power, or other essential services to force out a tenant is illegal in most states — it's harassment, not a landlord's right, even if rent is overdue.
If a landlord acts on a threat like this, you can approach local police (non-emergency line) or your state's Rent Control/tenancy authority — keep every message and receipt as evidence.

quiz.question: By what date must Bengaluru voters flagged in the draft SIR electoral roll verify their details to avoid being removed?
quiz.why: Voters flagged in a draft roll aren't automatically deleted — verifying or filing a claim during the correction window keeps them on the final list.

quiz.question: Bengaluru Metro's new Green and Pink Line trainsets are set for CMRS inspection trials on which dates?
quiz.why: CMRS (Commissioner of Metro Rail Safety) clearance is mandatory before any new metro trainset can carry passengers.

quiz.question: What did the Lok Sabha authorise this week regarding UPI transactions?
options: Permitting banks to levy charges on UPI transactions
Making UPI mandatory for all government payments
quiz.why: UPI transactions have largely been free for end users so far; this bill opens the door for banks to start charging fees on them.

quiz.question: What is the maximum term of India's Lok Sabha, unless it is dissolved earlier?
quiz.why: Unlike the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha is a permanent body — it's never dissolved, with about a third of its members retiring every two years.

quiz.question: What is the SI unit of electric current?
quiz.why: The ampere is named after André-Marie Ampère, a 19th-century French physicist who was a pioneer of classical electromagnetism.
